newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU telecoms firms gear up for 1998 deadline.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU telecoms firms gear up for 1998 deadline.

text.p: The privatisation of Telefonica de Espana takes place amid a frenzy of activity in the European Union telecommunications market as companies scramble to get in shape for a new era of free competition.

Telefonica itself is a key player in the European telecoms joint venture Unisource that was provisionally cleared by the European Commission last month, along with Unisource's global alliance with U.S. phone giant AT&T.
They are among a wave of deals that have been struck in the run-up to the January 1, 1998, deadline set by the EU for ending state telecoms monopolies in most of its 15 countries.

The Commission cleared the Global One trans-Atlantic alliance between France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and Sprint Corp last July and is now examining a planned merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp that was announced in November.

"It's quite clear that Europe will be looking at about four or five big telephone companies, with the others being marginal national or regional players," said Peter Alexiadis, a telecoms lawyer at Squire, Sanders and Dempsey in Brussels.

The 1998 deadline will force governments, which have been gradually liberalising their telecoms markets since the late 1980s under pressure from the Commission, to open up their lucrative voice phone sectors.
EU FINALISES LEGISLATIVE PACKAGE

While companies plot their strategy, the EU is rushing to wrap up a legislative package to regulate the new environment, covering issues such as telecoms licenses and ensuring access to affordable basic phone services.

Analysts said the EU was generally keeping to its liberalisation timetable, at least on paper, but warned that some important regulatory questions had still not been fully addressed, such as how to ensure that competitors have fair access to each other's networks.

"Just having the market open for competition still doesn't guarantee that you'll have a normal competitive functioning market from the first of January 1998, or ever," said Keith Mallinson, managing director of telecoms consultancy Yankee Group Europe.

He said new market players in some countries would face a tremendous challenge competing with the dominant presence and infrastructure of the traditional monopolies -- along the lines of trying to compete with Coca-Cola or Pepsi-Cola.
"You and I can start a cola company tomorrow but we'd still have the legacy of their overwhelming presence," he said.
But the move in Europe towards global alliances has given the Commission, the EU executive, a powerful weapon for prodding governments to do as much as they can to move the process along.
It agreed to clear the Global One venture, for example, only after Bonn and Paris pledged to open up their markets for telecoms infrastructure.

In deciding whether to clear the Unisource venture, it put pressure on Spain to renounce its right -- agreed by EU ministers during tough negotiations over the 1998 deadline -- to delay full telecoms liberalisation until 2003.
Madrid promised the Commission it would instead set a deadline of November 30, 1998.
ATTENTION TURNS TOWARD IMPLEMENTATION
The Commission has said that the telecoms legislative package was largely in place and it was now turning its attention to ensuring that the letter and spirit of the deadlines were followed.

"The real work is starting now," EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a recent conference. "The environment is in place, the legislation is there. But to make it happen in the real world is another thing."
Within the past few months, the Commission has issued long-awaited guidelines on "universal service" schemes and on "interconnection" agreements between competing phone operators.
The first outlined criteria that must be met by national financing schemes aimed at ensuring that affordable basic phone service is available to all residents.
The second, still in draft form, said the Commission could fine companies that did not allow competitors to hook up to their networks on fair terms.

The Commission has also closely policed the mobile phone market, for example telling Spain in December that it had until mid-March to announce how it planned to end a GSM licensing scheme that favoured Telefonica over the competing Airtel Movil consortium.
EU STILL TO ADOPT KEY LEGISLATION
The EU must still formally adopt several pieces of critical legislation, including rules on licensing telecoms operators in the new environment.

EU telecoms ministers have provisionally agreed a text, but it is now before the European Parliament, which has the power to negotiate changes with EU governments. Dutch public works minister Annemarie Jorritsma, who chairs the EU ministerial meetings, has urged the parliament to be flexible on measures needed to enforce the 1998 deadline.
"The newcomers on the market are trying very hard to prepare their business plans," she told the economic affairs committee. "They need the greatest amount of legal certainty."
But even with the rules in place, Alexiadis said, effective competition could be delayed while EU states implement their new licensing regimes.
"January 1, 1998 in most cases will be more realistically sometime in 1999," he said.
Some industry players -- British Telecom, for example -- say the EU will not fully realise its liberalisation plan until it creates some sort of pan-European telecoms regulatory authority.
They fear that national authorities will continue to favour their traditional operators or interpret EU rules differently.
But the Commission has shied away from making such a proposal, which would be highly controversial with some EU governments.

"The idea of a Euroregulator is going to come up again and again. Once we are beyond January 1, 1998 and have an idea about how things are developing -- then and only then can the debate really take off," Alexiadis said.
